extracted.intended_audience: 17th-century natural philosophers, observational astronomers, instrument-makers, and physicians
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and standards for recording and analysing observational astronomy (planetary spots, comets) and for designing/experimenting in optics (telescopes, prisms), plus exemplar clinical and natural-history case reporting. Emphasis on precise timings, positional reductions, experimental procedures, and practical evaluation of instrument designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prediction of Jovian spot returns (include temporal corrections)
rubrics_metrics.description: To find future times when the spot shall return to the midst of the belt, 'you are only to add always 9 hours and 56 minutes; and, for greater exactness, not to omit the ordinary equation of days, that depends on the inequality of the motion of the sun in respect of the equinoctial, nor the particular equation that depends on the inequality of the motion of Jupiter, according to the diversity of the distance of the sun and his apogee.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an observed epoch and add the mean revolution interval (9h56m) repeatedly, and include the equation of days and particular planetary inequalities to improve precision. Record epoch precisely (hours, minutes, seconds) and use it as basis for future predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a regular recurrent Jovian spot for longitude determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Because this revolution is very swift and regular, 'a traveller alone, even without having any correspondence with other observers, may make use of it to find the longitudes of the most remote places of the earth.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recurring, well-timed celestial phenomena can serve as portable longitude markers; later study required to establish achievable precision by this method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comet positional reporting against fixed stars
rubrics_metrics.description: Record comet positions by noting alignments and angular distances to named fixed stars, estimating apparent magnitude and angular size (minutes of degree), and then 'transfer this place of the comet upon the map of the fixed stars' to give ecliptic longitude and latitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give date and precise clock time, describe line-ups with bright stars, give distances in degrees/minutes to multiple reference stars, note tail orientation (relative to the sun), and compute coordinates (e.g., '23°25' of Taurus, in 14° N. lat.'). Include instrument used (e.g., telescope focal length) and naked-eye magnitude estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fitting observed comet places to a great circle and deriving orbital quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations of the comet 'fall into a line little differing from an arch of a great circle,' which allows determination of intersections with the ecliptic/equator and greatest declination; by choosing early observations and taking means one can find perigee timing and apparent daily motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select reliable observations (e.g., earliest ones), combine via means with other observers' data, fit to the apparent path (great circle approximation), and derive perigee date/time, daily motion (degrees per day), and maxima of declination — report method and intermediate choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precise time-stamping and epoch choice for observational astronomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations are given with precise times (hours, minutes, seconds) and an explicit epoch is chosen for future calculations (e.g., a particular night's observation 'being taken for the epocha').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide exact clock times for sightings, note observational limits (horizon, weather), and declare which observation is treated as epoch for subsequent predictions or reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative criteria for catadioptric telescope designs (Newton's considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton lists specific disadvantages of the Cassegrain-like design: greater light loss from the small convex speculum because of oblique incidence; the convex will not reflect truly unless hyperbolic (difficult to form); errors augmented by the long path between convex and eyepiece; requirement to keep tube no wider than necessary to place eyeglass near oval plane; perimeter errors augmented causing limited usable aperture; small convex requires extraordinary exactness; the little convex increases magnification disproportionately causing dark, confused images and restricted field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge telescope proposals by: how much light is lost at reflecting surfaces; the required accuracy of surface figures (hyperbolic vs plane); how errors are amplified by geometry and distances; resulting usable aperture, image brightness, field of view, ease of locating objects, and manufacturability of small, highly accurate surfaces. Prefer designs tested in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to prototypify and test instrument designs before divulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton: 'I could wish therefore, M. Cassegrain had tried his design, before he divulged it... if... he please hereafter to try it, I believe the success will inform him, that such projects are of little moment till they be put in practice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do practical trials and report empirical results before claiming advantages; theory alone may overlook manufacturability and practical defects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental protocols proposed to test Newton's theory of light (list of four experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed experiments: (1) contract beams of the sun without the hole of the window, and place prism between the focus of the lens and the hole; (2) cover both ends of the prism at several distances from the middle (or use movable rings) to see how that will vary the length of the figure; (3) move (rotate) the prism so that an end turns about while the middle stays steady; (4) move the prism by shoving it so that different parts pass over the hole, observing parallelism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the enumerated manipulations and note how the solar image's length and breadth vary with prism position/aperture and with rotation/translation of the prism. Report observations systematically for comparison with theory (Newton supplies expected qualitative outcomes for each proposal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed/expected outcomes for prism experiments (Newton's observations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Newton's observed responses: (1) an interposed prism between lens and focus draws the solar image out in length proportional to prism's distance from focus; (2) covering prism ends alters the breadth of the image proportional to the prism aperture without changing length; (3) rotating a single prism translates the coloured image along a circle (or conic) without altering shape (barring wall obliquity); (4) sliding the prism so different parts pass over the hole does not alter the phenomena appreciably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare experiment results to these expectations; note differences when using light from planets or stars (less inclined rays require lens collection). Use these observations to test/refine theoretical claims about refraction and dispersion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prism-pair alignment and imaging recommendations for refraction experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: For experiments destroying colour with two prisms: 'the long axes of the two prisms... be parallel one to another'; prisms must be 'placed very near to one another' or colours made before the second prism will not be destroyed; place a lens in the hole with its focus at the image Q or PT to make perimeters and straight edges better defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure precise geometric alignment (parallel faces, near contact) and use focusing optics to sharpen images. Report distances between prisms and lens/holes and the exact geometry used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collecting weak celestial light for prism experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: Because rays from Venus are less inclined one to another than those from the sun, Newton used a broad lens to collect her light and then interposed a prism between the lens and its focus, finding that a point-focus was drawn out into a long splendid line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When experimenting with weak or nearly parallel-source light (planets, stars), use larger collecting optics before interposition of dispersive elements to achieve observable effects. Anticipate weaker but analogous phenomena to solar experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for surgical/medical case reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The account of the sublingual stone includes history (suspected cause—long cold voyage), timeline of growth (about eight years), precipitating events (cold leading to swelling and purulent discharge), daily symptom chronology before incision (saliva characteristics across five days), operative details (incision, membranes coming away, stone description), and specimen characteristics (weight ≈7 grains, shape, surface, color).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report patient history and suspected etiology, chronology of symptoms and clinical signs with day-by-day detail when relevant, description of interventions and immediate clinical course, and physical description and measurements of excised specimens. Discuss differential diagnosis (ranula vs atheroma) and note related literature or prior instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for investigating 'animated horse-hairs' (natural-history debunking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lister examines prior literature, then reports dissecting beetles and finding hair-worms in their swollen bellies; he notes (1) worms crawled forth on incision; (2) survived in water many days and tried to escape; (3) movement is forward by head (distinguishable from tail); (4) measured lengths and thicknesses and described coloration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To test claims of spontaneous animation, combine literature review with direct experiment: examine candidate sources, dissect hosts, observe live behaviour in controlled conditions, measure morphology, and compare to existing taxonomic descriptions to attribute origin (parasitic insects) rather than spontaneous generation.
